Cape Canaveral, 2006-01-19. The fastest spacecraft ever launched at the time — 16.26 km/s relative to Earth — leaving Earth's gravity well at a velocity high enough to reach Jupiter in 13 months without a circular parking orbit. The trajectory was constrained by the launch window for the Pluto encounter ~9.5 years later; missing it would have added 5+ years.

Closest approach 2.3 million km from Jupiter on 2007-02-28. Used the encounter to test instruments and gain ~4 km/s of heliocentric velocity, cutting about three years off the cruise to Pluto. Bonus science: detailed atmospheric mapping, Io's volcanism, and the first imaging of the previously-unobserved Little Red Spot storm system.

Closest approach 12,500 km from Pluto's surface on 2015-07-14 — humanity's first close look at the dwarf planet system after a 9.5-year cruise. Revealed Sputnik Planitia (the heart-shaped nitrogen-ice plain), cryovolcanoes, and a thin atmosphere with haze layers. All five known Pluto moons imaged in the same encounter. Data downlink took 16 months at the 1-2 kbps far-distance rate.

Closest approach 3,538 km from Arrokoth on 2019-01-01 — the most distant flyby ever attempted at the time (43 AU from the Sun). The contact-binary structure of two roughly-spherical lobes joined at a narrow neck supported gentle-accretion models of planetesimal formation in the early solar system. Target found by HST in 2014 specifically to give New Horizons a post-Pluto secondary.
First flyby of Pluto and its moons; sharpest images of a Kuiper belt world

New Horizons had exactly one chance and took it. There was no orbit and no way to slow down — nine and a half years of travel, the fastest launch from Earth on record, all converging on a few hours at Pluto, executed by a machine so far away that each command took hours to arrive. It nailed the flyby on 14 July 2015 and overturned the expectation of a dead world: Pluto turned out to have mountains of water ice, a vast heart-shaped glacier of frozen nitrogen still slowly churning, and a young, active surface no one thought a body that small and cold could keep. Then it flew on to Arrokoth, a billion kilometres past Pluto — the most distant world ever seen up close — and it is still going.

A nine-year sprint after the fastest launch to date, New Horizons compressed decades of anticipation into one July 2015 day — a world turned from a pixelated blur into mountains of water ice and nitrogen glaciers on Pluto's heart-shaped Tombaugh Regio. The spacecraft later flew Arrokoth, linking the mission to the primordial solar system. Flight arcs in Orrery are direct-transfer teaching models, not the actual Jupiter gravity assist.
